preamble: Raising of the near-open front vowel [æ] to open-mid [ɛ] is documented in Southern Hemisphere Englishes and in the history of German. In New Zealand English TRAP rose from [æ] to [ɛ] as the first step of the short front vowel chain shift; South African English TRAP ranges from [æ] to [ɛ]; Broad Australian English shifts TRAP toward [ɛ]; and the Middle High German secondary-umlaut vowel ä [æ] was raised to [ɛ], so that ⟨ä⟩ is pronounced /ɛ/ in modern Standard German.

examples.note: In the short front vowel chain shift TRAP rose from near-open [æ] to open-mid [ɛ], while DRESS rose toward [e̝] and KIT centralized to [ə]; Cultivated NZE retains [æ].
TRAP ranges from [æ] to [ɛ] in General and Cultivated South African English and can be as close as [ɛ̝] in Broad SAE.
Speakers with the broad accent shift /æ/ and /æː/ toward [ɛ] and [ɛː]; many younger speakers instead lower TRAP to [a].

examples.from: Middle High German mähtec, secondary-umlaut ä [æ] (Old High German mahtīg)
examples.note: The Middle High German near-open ä [æ] produced by secondary umlaut was raised to [ɛ]; Standard German ⟨ä⟩ is pronounced /ɛ/ (formerly /æ/).
